Nvidia shares surged 31.5% on November 23 after news of Jensen Huang's reinstatement, underscoring how closely investor confidence in the company is tied to its co-founder. While near-term volatility is likely to persist, I remain decisively Bullish over the long term. Nvidia makes the chips, networking gear, and software powering the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and its earnings story is strong enough to ride out the ups and downs. Huang's return restores strategic continuity, but it does not restore trust overnight. Nvidia disclosed on November 12 that its co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) had resigned after the board accepted his resignation on November 11. The stock finished that session 4.3% lower. On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang had been reinstated, and the shares rose 31.5%. The episode highlighted a degree of key-person risk that I had underestimated. Nvidia's product cadence and customer confidence have always been closely tied to Huang. His return obviously removes the immediate succession problem. However, it leaves investors with a governance question. The board reinstated him before completing its independent investigation, shortly after creating a National Security and Export Control Committee on November 17 and alongside launching a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Those oversight steps are the right moves, but they do not excuse reversing a major leadership decision before the facts are settled. For my Bullish thesis, Huang's return is a stabilizer, though stronger governance is still required. Nvidia's results still point to very strong AI demand, and that's the part of the argument I find most compelling. Q3 FY2027 revenue was up 103% year-over-year to $115.8 billion, and Data Center revenue was up 110% to $107.6 billion. GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $2.70. Management has guided to around $130 billion in Q4 FY2027 revenue, plus or minus 3%, all the way through the end of the year, despite assuming zero Data Center compute revenue from China. Nvidia's product roadmap also gives me confidence the company can sustain growth. The company has started shipping Vera Rubin NVL72, with systems already operating at major cloud partners. This comes as some of its biggest customers continue to invest heavily in AI infrastructure. Meta (META), Google (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN) all raised their capital spending plans during their October earnings updates, suggesting that demand for the computing infrastructure Nvidia provides could remain strong. However, strong demand does not necessarily mean higher profitability. Nvidia expects its Q4 FY2027 gross margin to fall to 71%–72%, from about 75% in Q3 FY2027, as it ramps up its latest products. Competition is also rising, with Google's tensor processing units (TPUs) and Broadcom's (AVGO) custom chips offering alternatives to Nvidia's processors. While these developments deserve attention, I believe Nvidia's scale and rapid product cadence keep its long-term growth story intact. Nvidia's valuation is another reason I remain Bullish. At its November 25 closing price of $149.30, the stock traded at about a 15.52x forward price-to-earnings ratio (P/E), well below the 26.7x recorded at the end of Fiscal Year 2026 and 36.2x at the end of Fiscal Year 2025. The discount looks even more compelling when compared with its peers. AVGO trades at 25.82x forward P/E, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) commands a much higher multiple of 50.24x. Of course, some discount may be justified given the recent governance concerns. However, I believe the current valuation is becoming hard to ignore, especially considering Nvidia's market position and continued earnings growth. Nvidia does not need to return to its previous multiples for investors to see meaningful upside over the next year. If earnings continue to meet expectations, the stock has room to recover, which further supports my Buy stance. The biggest risk to my bullish view is that Nvidia's earnings growth may not meet expectations. If the major tech companies start to scale back their AI infrastructure spend, then we could see weaker demand and margin pressure for Nvidia. Competition from custom AI chips is also still an issue. Beyond the financials, Jensen Huang's 11-day departure and return have highlighted a very real level of key-man risk that I find hard to ignore. His return may have been enough to quell immediate investor angst, but it doesn't mitigate the governance issues. If those issues continue to fester or start to impact the business, then I would have to reconsider my Buy. Turning to Wall Street, Nvidia carries a Strong Buy consensus rating on TipRanks, based on 34 Buys, nine Holds, and one Sell over the past three months. The average analyst price target is $234. Relative to the November 25 closing price of $149.30, that implies about 56.73% upside over the next 12 months. A recent TipRanks article highlighted the Street's renewed optimism following Huang's return. Citi (C) analyst Atif Malik reiterated his Buy rating and raised his price target to $240 from $225, arguing that Huang's reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership and should help restore confidence in its product roadmap. Goldman Sachs (GS) analyst James Schneider also reaffirmed his Buy rating and maintained a $220 price target. Wall Street's Strong Buy consensus, even with analysts flagging ongoing governance overhangs, matches my own view. I'm not predicting the next move in Nvidia's share price. However, over the next 12-month period, I think the combination of strong earnings power and a sharply compressed valuation more than offsets the governance and geopolitical risks, as long as the business continues to execute. title: Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before CEO Jensen Huang Testifies in Front of Congress on Dec. 1 and Dec. 3? - The Motley Fool
content: Huang is set to testify before Congress next week, both publicly and behind closed doors. Jensen Huang may be back as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), but the chip giant's worries are far from over, as regulators and lawmakers continue to investigate whether Nvidia breached export controls and whether Huang's relationship with a Singaporean data center executive may have posed national security risks. Huang and other Nvidia executives are set to testify before Congress next week on the above concerns, which the entire stock market will be watching. On Dec. 1, Huang will testify before the U.S. House of Representatives' Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committee, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Nvidia's General Counsel Tim Teter will also testify before the same committees on Dec. 2. Both hearings will be private, with transcripts not expected to be published publicly for some time. But on Dec. 3, Huang will testify at a live hearing before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, an event that will be closely monitored by all investors. Should investors buy Nvidia stock before these hearings? While President Donald Trump has come out in support of Huang and claims to have played a role in his reinstatement, the hearings will help reveal how other lawmakers feel about Huang and what's going on with Nvidia. "The market volatility and nervousness is centered on a number of issues that the Jensen soap opera has highlighted front and center," Yorkville Ives analyst and Managing Partner Dan Ives wrote in a recent research note, according to Business Insider. "Next week Jensen carries the weight of the entire tech sector and AI Revolution thesis when he marches into DC." When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $2,799,718*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Huang's reinstatement as CEO led to a swift surge in the stock, but since then, shares have been pressured by lingering investor concerns about the company. Multiple reports suggest that a woman Huang had an affair with, named Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at the Singaporean data center company MegaSpeed, may have facilitated a network that diverted advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese firms. Investors are trying to understand how much prior demand for Nvidia's chips, if any, may have been driven by similar sources. Since the scandal came to light, the U.S. Commerce Department has moved to close loopholes and tighten export controls that may have allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia chips remotely. The Commerce Department is now also requiring companies in select countries, such as Singapore and Indonesia, to obtain a license before transferring or reexporting advanced chips from U.S. companies. In his note, Ives said he believes the impact on revenue resulting from such export controls is "a containable 15% to 20% at most." Still, that's a significant amount, and while some of it is priced in, Nvidia stock could certainly face more pressure if it believed future demand wouldn't be as strong. Given that Wall Street analysts like Ives are already contemplating what would happen to Nvidia's revenue if increased export restrictions lower demand, or some sources of demand abroad are closed off, it's clear the market is pricing in at least some of the potential impact. Still, Wall Street consensus estimates expect Nvidia to earn $16.61 per share on an adjusted basis for its fiscal year 2028 ending in late January 2028. That means Nvidia trades at just 9x forward earnings, so the valuation is attractive. But as we've seen through this whole debacle, things can change in a hurry, so I would never tell investors to buy a stock based on a near-term event like a Congressional hearing. With Nvidia trading at a cheap level, I think investors can purchase a position to hold long term. But I do not believe that the majority of a traditional stock portfolio should be concentrated in Nvidia or AI stocks, as much uncertainty remains. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google’s CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity. title: Fire Sale: Here's Why Now May Be the Perfect Time to Buy Nvidia Stock - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia's stock is trading at levels not seen in years. There are multiple reasons why Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) is a great stock to buy right now, but investors must understand the risks, too. Fortunately, one of those risks just went away with Jensen Huang returning to the CEO position. At the end of the day, I think Nvidia's stock is still trading at fire-sale prices. I think now is the perfect time to swoop in and scoop up shares, as a deal this good won't last forever. The Nvidia turmoil has been notable lately. It all started with co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang resigning from his position after admitting being unfaithful to his wife. But then the board reinstated him a few days later. But he's not out of hot water yet, as he must appear before Congress to testify on Nvidia's chip shipments. A woman he’s alleged to have had an affair with is rumored to be a Chinese spy. Another issue with Nvidia right now is concerns about how accurate its financials are regarding chip sales to China. The U.S. has banned the export of some types of chips. What was legally allowed to be sent directly to China was $2.4 billion for Nvidia in Q3, and it is no longer shipping these products to China. But what makes investors worried is how many chips were being sold to companies in other countries that were illegally diverting them to China. There are a handful of government entities that are probing Nvidia for these allegations, which could bring about fines. This comes with a risk of Nvidia potentially losing sales to some of these companies, which could affect Nvidia's total revenue. However, I’m not worried. If there were a massive and obvious part of Nvidia's business that was being sold internationally that didn't add up to what domestic companies were spending on AI, this would have raised red flags long ago. While I think there may have been some (maybe a percent or two) of sales that ended up in places that they weren't supposed to be, the majority of Nvidia's revenue base is fine, and the companies behind that revenue base look like they are going to spend more next year. After the catastrophic sell-off, Nvidia's stock now trades for about 14 times earnings as I write this. For reference, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) trades for about 20 times trailing earnings. So, even without any growth baked into the stock, Nvidia is trading at a discount to the broader stock market. When you factor in next year's estimated growth, this gets even more mismatched. During its Q3 conference call, then-interim CEO Colette Kress raised next year's revenue growth guidance from 70% to 75%. The reason is obvious: The AI hyperscalers are spending more and more on AI. This isn't going to change, and Nvidia's products practically sell themselves. When you factor in next year's potential growth, the stock trades for an unbelievable 9.3 times next year's earnings estimates. Those price tags are reserved for companies where failure is imminent or that have single-digit revenue growth. Nvidia is neither, and I think this fire sale could be one of the greatest opportunities to invest in Nvidia since the start of the AI arms race in 2023. While there will be some scary headlines that appear about Nvidia over the next few months, I think it will emerge OK, making now a perfect time to load up on shares, hold onto them for a few years, and massively profit. title: Jensen Huang Says Business as Usual at Nvidia ($NVDA) while Samson Mow Pushes for Bitcoin focused Board Seat - Crowdfund Insider
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has recently found itself at the intersection of internal leadership reaffirmation and an unsolicited external suggestion for capital allocation. In addition to these developments, Samson Mow, chief executive of the Bitcoin-focused technology firm JAN3, publicly stated his willingness to join the semiconductor company’s board of directors. He expressed readiness to support chief executive Jensen Huang in pursuing an assertive approach that would direct a substantial portion of Nvidia’s cash holdings toward Bitcoin. Mow’s comments appeared on the social platform X around November 23–24. He indicated that the chipmaker’s cash position, reported near $29 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of late October in quarterly filings, should not remain entirely in conventional currency instruments that lose purchasing power over time. Instead, he argued the moment had arrived for the company to acquire Bitcoin as part of its treasury operations. The suggestion followed Nvidia’s recent board decision to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive, and director after a brief period of absence. This external proposal arrived against a backdrop of Huang’s return to day-to-day leadership. Huang’s reinstatement followed a short interruption triggered by personal matters that had drawn public attention. In his first company-wide employee gathering after returning, Huang offered expressions of regret for the disruption and indicated he had begun counseling. At the same time, he conveyed that the company’s overall direction would remain largely consistent with its prior course. According to reporting cited in a LinkedIn News summary, observers familiar with internal discussions expect operations under this renewed tenure to resemble the established model rather than undergo major strategic shifts. The approach appears intended to steady investor sentiment amid ongoing market sensitivity surrounding artificial intelligence growth projections. Huang also addressed the topic of leadership continuity during the staff meeting. He stated that formal succession planning would introduce unnecessary layers of hierarchy within the organization. He pointed to Nvidia’s distinctive operating structure, in which numerous senior executives oversee discrete areas of the business and report in a relatively flat arrangement. In his view, this setup already provides multiple capable individuals who could assume broader responsibilities if needed, without designating a single heir apparent in advance. The comments align with earlier indications that Huang has long viewed traditional succession frameworks as potentially counterproductive for the company’s culture and decision-making speed. Market participants and analysts had previously noted the absence of a clearly identified internal successor as a source of risk when Huang stepped aside earlier in the month. Nvidia’s share price experienced volatility during that interval before recovering upon confirmation of his return. The company has emphasized continuity of strategy and execution to address concerns about the durability of artificial-intelligence demand and related capital expenditure cycles. Looking ahead, Huang is expected to confront questions on national-security considerations and corporate-governance practices in upcoming congressional appearances. These inquiries stem from the circumstances surrounding his temporary departure and broader scrutiny of advanced chip technologies in geopolitical contexts. The board has stated that it received input from senior U.S. government levels and concluded that reinstatement presented no national-security concern, yet legislative oversight is anticipated to continue. Nvidia’s latest financial disclosures show cash and equivalents rising sharply through the year, accompanied by significant share repurchases and dividend distributions. Mow’s proposal highlights one possible use for residual liquidity, though no indication has emerged that the company is evaluating digital asset allocations. The suggestion remains an individual initiative rather than a formal shareholder resolution or board-level discussion. Taken together, the developments illustrate Nvidia’s emphasis on operational continuity under Huang’s restored leadership while external observers float alternative ideas for deploying capital. The company continues to project confidence in its existing model even as it navigates governance expectations and market perceptions of long-term AI-related risks. Jensen Huang's return as CEO doesn't make Nvidia (NVDA) stock a Buy, despite the market's positive reaction. Shares of the leading semiconductor manufacturer jumped roughly 31.5% on November 23 after Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang with immediate effect. Yet the stock remains down roughly 31% over the past month following a steep sell-off. Although Nvidia enjoys a long runway for growth, I believe investors should closely watch the regulatory scrutiny still surrounding the company. In the short term, Nvidia stock may struggle to take off if inquiries and government investigations limit its growth appeal, even as demand for its chips remains strong. As a result, I am turning Neutral on Nvidia because I believe its valuation already reflects both its strong chip demand and the regulatory and macro risks ahead. I believe investors should brace themselves for increased regulatory scrutiny in the coming months, which is one of the main reasons behind my Neutral stance on the company. There are early warning signs. On November 17, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is conducting a probe into Nvidia to look into its accounting practices and public disclosures to determine whether the chip giant has misled investors. On November 20, The New York Times (NYT) provided more details on this alleged SEC probe. Specifically, the inquiry is looking into whether Nvidia's 2025 change in how it reports regional results has misled investors. Last year, the company switched from reporting revenue based on customer billing addresses to customer corporate headquarters. This shift entirely removed Singapore as a standalone geographic market for the company. Given Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, who was the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed, the SEC probe is likely to scrutinize this personal relationship. If Nvidia is found to have misled investors, the SEC may penalize the company with fines and even force it to restate its financials. Both outcomes will negatively affect shareholder sentiment. In addition to the SEC probe, I believe investors should pay close attention to the ongoing government probe of Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Before CEO Huang's reinstatement, President Trump wrote in a social media post, "Attorney General Todd Blanche has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." Although President Trump's remarks sound promising, this does not mark the end of government scrutiny. The U.S. Department of Justice and the Commerce Department are conducting a criminal export-control investigation into Singapore-based Megaspeed. The objective of this investigation is to determine whether Nvidia's artificial intelligence (AI) chips were diverted through Megaspeed to Chinese companies and China's state-owned military contractors. As confirmed by National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, Alice Huang is directly under investigation as part of this probe. While the Justice Department recently stated it found no evidence of wrongdoing by Jensen Huang regarding his relationship with Alice Huang, federal prosecutors are still investigating her former firm, Megaspeed, over potential export-control violations. In addition, on December 1, Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear before the House Intelligence Committee, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Select Committee on China. Beyond the regulatory threats Nvidia faces, I believe investor sentiment toward the company is likely to remain weak, given ongoing scrutiny of aggressive AI investments by hyperscalers and tech giants. The biggest macro risk is that AI investments are outpacing earnings. A quick look at hyperscalers' EBITDA and capex reveals why investors are worried. According to Morningstar (MORN) data, capex as a percentage of EBITDA among Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN), Meta Platforms, Inc. (META), Alphabet Inc. (GOOG), and Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) averaged just 43% in 2024. This ratio ballooned to 60% in 2025, with estimates pointing to a further expansion of this ratio to 90% this year. At the same time, Morningstar expects the incremental EBITDA yield on prior-year capex to fall from 50% in 2025 to 39% in 2026, underscoring that earnings realization is lagging behind capital deployment. These projections suggest that hyperscalers are spending heavily on AI with the expectation of fully realizing the returns only over the longer term. Massive upfront outlays for chips, data centers, and power infrastructure will continue to pressure free cash flows (FCFs) and push big tech companies to issue more debt. That dynamic does not bode well for Nvidia, as any move by hyperscalers to moderate spending to protect FCF would directly hit the chipmaker's revenue. Nvidia is currently valued at a forward P/E multiple of just 16x. That is well below its five-year average of 40.99x. The multiple looks cheap for a company that nearly doubled revenue over the 12 months ended October 31. I believe this seemingly cheap valuation is a classic cyclical trap rather than a bargain today. My caution centers on three specific risks. First, the active SEC review into accounting practices and geographic revenue disclosures creates unquantifiable legal and restatement risk. Second, a slowdown in hyperscaler AI spending will compress forward EPS estimates for Nvidia meaningfully. Third, increased scrutiny on chip exports may deteriorate investor sentiment before we see an improvement. Until regulators clarify disclosure questions and hyperscaler return on invested capital proves durable without vendor-financing support, I prefer waiting for clearer earnings visibility before adding to my position. Based on the ratings of 44 Wall Street analysts, the average Nvidia price target is $234, which implies upside of roughly 57% from the current market price, according to TipRanks data. Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO on November 23 sent its stock higher, as expected. Contrary to popular belief, I believe CEO Huang's return to the company does not solve the regulatory threats faced by the company. In fact, I believe regulatory scrutiny will only increase with his return as CEO. Nvidia is entering a period of legal chaos at a time when investors are questioning the durability of aggressive AI spending by hyperscalers. Together, these challenges are likely to keep Nvidia stock under pressure in the foreseeable future. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results
